rv.q: He’s so unsettling during this scene (scarier than the box of rats waiting for Winston in Room 101 of the Ministry of Love) that Orwell’s suggestion that Big Brother doesn’t actually exist — that he is, in fact, all of us — really knocks us out.
The result is a punishingly intense evening of theater that will leave you shaken—and should leave you thinking as well.
The show memorably reinvents one of the most terrifying tales of modern times.
What makes this antipropaganda broadside so lastingly compelling is how successfully it resists decaying into propaganda itself.
The production succeeds in creating a palpably oppressive atmosphere that makes the audience complicit in Winston's suffocating world of surveillance and thought control.
In their version, no one — and I mean no one — is to be trusted as a reliable witness.
A brutal, nightmarish telling of a cautionary novel.
The torture scenes are visceral, ghastly, and hair-raisingly vivid.

But this emphatic adaptation of the seminal George Orwell novel, written and directed by rising British stage talents Robert Icke and Duncan Macmillan, reaches heights of punishing intensity that will rattle even the most jaded audiences.
In a grim irony, this all makes for the kind of evening that doesn’t so much stimulate thought as shut it down, since the meanings have been so carefully parsed and served up for us.
The effort to freak out the audience is taken to such extremes in Icke and Macmillan’s grim British-born production that this “1984” manages nothing so successfully as upstaging Orwell himself.
Broadway’s 1984. Is an Electrifying Fable With a Message for the Resistance
In 2017, "1984" resonates louder than ever.

Those who don’t have time to pick up the book (or didn’t read it in high school) can check out the streamlined, multimedia-enhanced, unapologetically intense production (adapted and directed by Robert Icke and Duncan Macmillan) on Broadway.

So important is the philosophy. So relevant is the message. So important is an awareness of the way we are manipulated with language and that those in power control that language and how we view … everything.
That production is a picnic compared to this nightmare vision of the alternative future.
To some degree, the strobe lights, gunshots and gore become such a distraction from the story that they threaten to overwhelm its dire message about government run amok.
The result is that significant stretches of this "1984" are plainly boring.
This 1984 is designed to pummel you into submission, and it succeeds so thoroughly that you may find yourself wondering whether you've been entertained or merely endured something.
For all its moving set pieces, along with a busy, ear-blasting soundscape, frequent blackouts, blinding lights and live video, it's strangely unmoving and low-impact.

cn.t: Critics find this visceral adaptation of Orwell's dystopian novel punishingly intense and unnervingly timely, though some question whether its relentless brutality prioritizes style over substance.

sg.ra: SeatPlan, TickPick and Headout all converge: center rows D-K sit at a perfect distance to take in the whole stage without craning. Row A is called out as too close for comfortable viewing. Dress Circle overhangs at Orchestra row L and the Mezz overhang only becomes obvious at row R without significantly cutting the stage, so the middle band is protected. 2017 ATG restoration upgraded legroom throughout.

SeatPlan flags Dress Circle A-B center as offering unobstructed sightlines and the 'front few rows of the Center Dress Circle' as premium; rows D-F center are repeatedly called out as great-value seats with full sweep of the stage. The 258-seat section has a good rake and generous legroom. Balcony overhang only becomes obvious at row J and doesn't cut into the stage, so every row is usable.

SeatPlan describes Balcony rows A-B center as hanging close enough for detailed views and reports sightlines 'better than average' for a third level. Rear rows G-H are the cheapest in the house. Rake is very good, but legroom is tighter than the rest of the theater and the top of the stage may be cut by the balcony's angle. AVFMS user at G110 noted that some in-audience action isn't visible from rear balcony.
